claim: Excitation is balanced by inhibition in neuronal networks.
source: Excitation is balanced by inhibition in neuronal networks (Andersen et al., 1963).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andersen et al., 1963

claim: In cortical circuits, feedforward inhibition is rapidly and robustly recruited by excitatory inputs.
source: In cortical circuits, feedforward inhibition is rapidly and robustly recruited by excitatory inputs, while pyramidal neuron firing elicits feedback inhibition to further dampen excitability (Alle et al., 2001; Lamsa et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Pouille and Scanziani, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Alle et al., 2001; Lamsa et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Pouille and Scanziani, 2004)

claim: Pyramidal neuron firing elicits feedback inhibition to further dampen excitability.
source: In cortical circuits, feedforward inhibition is rapidly and robustly recruited by excitatory inputs, while pyramidal neuron firing elicits feedback inhibition to further dampen excitability (Alle et al., 2001; Lamsa et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Pouille and Scanziani, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Inhibition strongly controls synaptic plasticity, a putative cellular mechanism of learning.
source: Furthermore, inhibition strongly controls synaptic plasticity, a putative cellular mechanism of learning (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Whitlock et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Whitlock et al., 2006

claim: Intact inhibition limits potentiation to relatively low levels.
source: Intact inhibition limits potentiation to relatively low levels while pharmacologically blocking inhibition facilitates both the induction and magnitude of potentiation (Artola and Singer, 1987; Bear et al., 1992; Steward et al., 1990; Wigström and Gustafsson, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Pharmacologically blocking inhibition facilitates both the induction and magnitude of potentiation.
source: Intact inhibition limits potentiation to relatively low levels while pharmacologically blocking inhibition facilitates both the induction and magnitude of potentiation (Artola and Singer, 1987; Bear et al., 1992; Steward et al., 1990; Wigström and Gustafsson, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Inhibition suppression is a potential mechanism for enhancing learning by favoring synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons.
source: Thus, inhibition suppression is a potential mechanism for enhancing learning by favoring synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons.
evidence: Inferred from previous statements about inhibition's role in controlling plasticity

claim: CA1 fast-spiking putative interneurons are suppressed when rats explore a novel spatial environment.
source: CA1 fast-spiking putative interneurons are suppressed when rats explore a novel spatial environment (Frank et al., 2004; Nitz and McNaughton, 2004; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Learning new food locations in a familiar environment dynamically modulated fast-spiking interneuron activity and altered the associations of these interneurons with pyramidal cell ensembles.
source: Learning new food locations in a familiar environment dynamically modulated fast-spiking interneuron activity and altered the associations of these interneurons with pyramidal cell ensembles (Dupret et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dupret et al., 2013

claim: Hippocampal CA3 parvalbumin-expressing interneurons have decreased network connectivity during the initial learning of the Morris Water Maze.
source: Hippocampal CA3 parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PV-ints) have decreased network connectivity during the initial learning of the Morris Water Maze, but this connectivity increases with task performance, a modulation that is is necessary for learning (Donato et al., 2013; Ruediger et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donato et al., 2013; Ruediger et al., 2011

claim: CA3 PV-int connectivity increases with task performance in the Morris Water Maze, a modulation that is necessary for learning.
source: Hippocampal CA3 parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PV-ints) have decreased network connectivity during the initial learning of the Morris Water Maze, but this connectivity increases with task performance, a modulation that is is necessary for learning (Donato et al., 2013; Ruediger et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donato et al., 2013; Ruediger et al., 2011

claim: Suppression of somatostatin- and/or parvalbumin-expressing interneurons is necessary for certain types of cortical and amygdalar learning.
source: Furthermore, numerous studies have shown that suppression of somatostatin- and/or parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (SOM-ints and PV-ints) is necessary for certain types of cortical and amygdalar learning. This suppression is often triggered by disinhibitory inputs from interneurons that preferentially target other interneurons for inhibition, including vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons (VIP-ints) (Gentet et al., 2012; Karnani et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2013; Letzkus et al., 2011; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Mardinly et al., 2016; Pi et al., 2013; Turi et al., 2019; Wolff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Disinhibitory inputs from VIP-expressing interneurons often trigger suppression of SOM-ints and PV-ints during learning.
source: This suppression is often triggered by disinhibitory inputs from interneurons that preferentially target other interneurons for inhibition, including vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons (VIP-ints) (Gentet et al., 2012; Karnani et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2013; Letzkus et al., 2011; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Mardinly et al., 2016; Pi et al., 2013; Turi et al., 2019; Wolff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The activity or plasticity of numerous other interneuron cell-types has been implicated in controlling animal behaviors.
source: Finally, the activity or plasticity of numerous other interneuron cell-types has been implicated in controlling animal behaviors (Basu et al., 2016; Hartzell et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Basu et al., 2016; Hartzell et al., 2018

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons show transient suppression in firing during exploration of novel environments.
source: These studies found transient suppression in firing of fast-spiking units during exploration of novel environments, consistent with a model in which decreased inhibition is permissive for excitatory plasticity and downstream learning.
evidence: Inferred from previous citations about fast-spiking interneuron suppression in novel environments

claim: Studies using calcium imaging in head-fixed animals in visual virtual reality contexts have found conflicting results with freely moving animals regarding PV-int activity in new environments.
source: Interestingly, studies using calcium imaging in head-fixed animals in visual virtual reality (VR) contexts have found conflicting results with freely moving animals, with either no change in PV-int calcium activity in new virtual environments or a decrease in somatic calcium activity coupled with increased putative axonal calcium fluorescence, both suggesting no decrease in perisomatic inhibition (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Sheffield et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Sheffield et al., 2017

claim: SOM-ints selectively innervate the dendrites of pyramidal neurons and can directly control dendritic excitability.
source: SOM-ints, although far less understood, are of interest because they selectively innervate the dendrites of pyramidal neurons and can directly control dendritic excitability.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SOM-int anatomy and function

claim: Dendritic spikes can mediate long-term plasticity, place field formation, and learning.
source: Dendritic spikes, typically characterized by calcium entry through Ca2+ channels or NMDA receptors, generate burst firing of neurons and can mediate long-term plasticity, place field formation, and learning (Bittner et al., 2015; Bittner et al., 2017; Cichon and Gan, 2015; Golding et al., 2002; Larkum et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Formation of place fields is associated with dendritic spikes that occur during transient periods of SOM-int activity suppression in novel environments.
source: Formation of place fields is associated with dendritic spikes that occur during transient periods of SOM-int activity suppression in novel environments (Sheffield et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheffield et al., 2017

claim: SOM-int activation rather than suppression is required for fear learning in CA1 or in the dentate gyrus.
source: In contrast, SOM-int activation rather than suppression is required for fear learning, both in CA1 or in the dentate gyrus (Lovett-Barron et al., 2014; Stefanelli et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lovett-Barron et al., 2014; Stefanelli et al., 2016

claim: Extracellular electrode recordings are typically stable for a few hours and have limited ability to identify interneurons.
source: This is partially a technical issue as extracellular electrode recordings are typically stable for a few hours and have limited ability to identify interneurons, making the longitudinal recording of single interneuron activity difficult.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of electrophysiology limitations

claim: Many inhibitory interneurons are strongly influenced by pyramidal neurons, driven in a feedforward and/or feedback manner.
source: Many inhibitory interneurons are strongly influenced by pyramidal neurons, driven in a feedforward and/or feedback manner.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of circuit connectivity

claim: Individual interneurons within the same cell-type show functional diversity in their locomotion-related activity.
source: Previous work from our lab and others have found functional diversity within the same putative interneuronal cell-types, with individual neurons being consistently activated or inhibited by locomotion (Arriaga and Han, 2017; Garcia-Junco-Clemente et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arriaga and Han, 2017; Garcia-Junco-Clemente et al., 2019

claim: Water-scheduled mice were trained to run to alternating ends of a virtual visual track to receive water rewards.
source: We initially trained water-scheduled mice to run to alternating ends of a virtual visual track to receive water rewards, using their movement on a floating spherical treadmill (styrofoam ball) to control their movement in VR (Arriaga and Han, 2017; Dombeck et al., 2010; Harvey et al., 2009).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Mice need to physically rotate and run on the ball in order to turn and maneuver through VR.
source: Note that mice need to physically rotate and run on the ball in order to turn and maneuvre through VR, making this an internally consistent and continuous virtual world that contrasts with VR tasks requiring unidirectional movement on a track with either 'teleportation' back to the starting point after each trial (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Sato et al., 2017; Sheffield et al., 2017) or an infinitely repeating corridor (Gauthier and Tank, 2018).
evidence: Description of experimental setup and comparison to other VR paradigms

claim: Upon initial exposure to the New virtual world, animal behavior was dramatically altered.
source: Upon initial exposure to the New virtual world, animal behavior was dramatically altered.
evidence: Observation from experimental data

claim: Performance in New was significantly worse on Days 1, 2, and 4 compared to FamAve.
source: Performance in New was significantly worse on Days 1, 2, and 4 compared to FamAve (the average performance in the flanking Fam and Fam′ epochs) (Figure 1C, performance in New normalized to FamAve).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Task impairment in New was largest on Day 1 and gradually decreased over the next four days of exposure.
source: This impairment was largest on Day 1 and gradually decreased over the next four days of exposure to the same 'New' world, indicating that animals learned to adapt previously learned behavior to the new context.
evidence: Observation from experimental data

claim: Mice lick with higher frequency outside of the reward window in New compared to familiar environments.
source: Similarly, animals in familiar environments generally begin licking within a 1 s window centered on reward delivery (which we define as 'correct' licks); in comparison, mice lick with higher frequency outside of this window in New (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Day 1, p<0.01, t = −4.82; Day 2, p<0.05, t = −3.13), with their behavior improving over repeated training.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A with statistical tests

claim: The time course of behavioral recovery was the same for both new environments (New 1 and New 2).
source: We found that the time course of behavioral recovery was the same for both new environments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), suggesting context-dependence.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: There was no significant difference in behavioral performance between the flanking Fam and Fam′ epochs.
source: We also confirmed there was no significant difference in behavioral performance (using non-normalized rew/min) between the flanking Fam and Fam′ epochs, indicating that time-dependent effects such as satiation or fatigue were not responsible for task impairment in the intervening New epoch (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H

claim: SOM-int neuronal activity was strongly suppressed upon transition into New.
source: SOM-int neuronal activity, measured as ΔF/F, was strongly suppressed upon transition into New (ΔF/F of 6 sample cells from one imaging plane of one mouse, Figure 2A; Video 1 shows activity suppression in another set of SOM-ints).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Video 1

claim: Individual SOM-int neurons were differentially suppressed with some being relatively unaffected.
source: Individual neurons were differentially suppressed with some being relatively unaffected.
evidence: Observation from experimental data

claim: On returning to Familiar after New in Fam′, SOM-int calcium activity rapidly recovered.
source: On returning to Familiar after New in Fam′, calcium activity rapidly recovered, as did behavioral performance (example cells and behavior from an additional three animals in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: SOM-int activity exhibited significant suppression in New that gradually decreased over days.
source: Indeed, SOM-int activity exhibited significant suppression in New that gradually decreased over days (Day 1, p<0.001, t = −8.70; Day 2, p<0.05, t = −4.06).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests on experimental data

claim: The decrease in SOM-int suppression paralleled the increase in behavioral performance in New.
source: This decrease in suppression paralleled the increase in behavioral performance in New, as normalized to the average performance in Fam and Fam′ (Figure 2F, performance worse in New on Days 1 and 4, p<0.05, Day 1 t = −4.34, Day 4 t = −5.57).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F with statistical tests

claim: SOM-int neurite activity was similarly suppressed as somatic activity.
source: By analyzing regions of interest in the statum oriens that included neurites and excluded somata, we found that SOM-int neurite activity was similarly suppressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: In familiar environments, locomotion-related variables had relatively high correlation with SOM-int activity.
source: As a first pass, we individually correlated these variables with cellular activity and found that, in familiar environments, locomotion-related variables had relatively high correlation with activity, on average.
evidence: Analysis of experimental data

claim: In new environments, correlations between locomotion-related variables and SOM-int activity were much lower.
source: In new environments, these correlations were much lower, indicating a disruption in the relationship between behavioral variables and neuronal activity in new environments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Model fit was significantly worse in New versus FamAve for all 5 days.
source: Using both measures, we found that model fit was significantly worse in New versus FamAve for all 5 days, suggesting that changes in behavior, including locomotion, did not explain decreased ΔF/F in New (RMS error, Figure 3B; R2, Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B and 3C

claim: GLMs trained on behavioral variables in New were still very poor at predicting activity in New.
source: In fact, GLMs trained on behavioral variables in New were still very poor at predicting activity in New (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), whereas in contrast, GLMs trained in either Fam and Fam′ predicted activity in familiar environments well, but poorly in New.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: The strong suppression of SOM-int activity in new environments is not simply explained by changes in mouse behavior but is likely to be triggered by contextual novelty itself.
source: Taken together, these data show that the strong suppression of SOM-int activity in new environments is not simply explained by changes in mouse behavior but is likely to be triggered by contextual novelty itself.
evidence: Inference from GLM modeling results

claim: PV-int somatic calcium activity was strongly suppressed in New and recovered with repeated exposure to New.
source: Similar to SOM-ints, PV-int somatic calcium activity was also strongly suppressed in New and recovered with repeated exposure to New (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Suppression of activity seemed even stronger in PV-ints compared to SOM-ints.
source: Qualitatively, suppression of activity seemed even stronger in PV-ints, perhaps reflecting decreased activity from a higher starting firing rate, as PV-ints generally have greater basal firing rate in vivo (Royer et al., 2012; Varga et al., 2012).
evidence: Observation from data with citation support for baseline firing rates

claim: There was a spectrum of activity suppression in individual PV-ints, ranging from strong suppression to moderate activation in New.
source: There was also a spectrum of activity suppression in individual PV-ints, ranging from strong suppression to moderate activation in New (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: PV-int neurites were suppressed in New.
source: Firing fields of PV-ints were broad in both environments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and, similar to cell somata, PV-int neurites were suppressed in New (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: The 'No Task' environment evoked strong suppression of SOM-int activity, similar to the suppression seen when mice are switched into New.
source: The 'No Task' environment evoked strong suppression of SOM-int activity, similar to the suppression seen when mice are switched into New (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A–D

claim: Over 5 days of exposure to the same 'No Task' environment, SOM-int activity remained strongly suppressed.
source: However, over 5 days of exposure to the same 'No Task' environment, activity remained strongly suppressed (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The same cells from the same mice showed strong recovery of activity over 5 days of exposure to New.
source: In marked contrast, the same cells from the same mice showed strong recovery of activity over 5 days of exposure to New (Figure 5E, showing data from six mice used in Figure 2 that were also, later, switched into the 'No Task' environment).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Recovery of SOM-int activity is unlikely to be the result of habituation to surprise and may rather depend on the recovery of task performance in the new context.
source: Thus, recovery of SOM-int activity is unlikely to be the result of habituation to surprise and may rather depend on the recovery of task performance in the new context.
evidence: Inference from comparison of New and No Task conditions

claim: SOM-ints show stable short-time population correlation in Fam that drops significantly on the first day of New.
source: SOM-ints show stable short-time population correlation in Fam that drops significantly on the first day of New, with a return to high short-time population correlation on return to Fam′.
evidence: Analysis of population correlation data

claim: By the second day of New, SOM-int population activity shows similar levels of correlation across Fam, New, and Fam′.
source: By the second day of New, population activity shows similar levels of correlation across Fam, New, and Fam′ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: SOM-ints in 'No Task' periods show low short-time population correlation, which remains depressed throughout 5 days of exposure.
source: In contrast, SOM-ints in 'No Task' periods show low short-time population correlation, which remains depressed throughout 5 days of exposure (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D

claim: PV-ints in new environments showed loss of short-time population correlation in New relative to Fam, and this decrease was significant for all 5 days.
source: PV-ints in new environments also showed loss of short-time population correlation in New relative to Fam, although unlike SOM-ints, this decrease was significant for all 5 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F

claim: There was strong correlation between activity suppression in New 1 vs. New 2 in individual SOM-ints.
source: To the contrary, we found strong correlation between activity suppression in New 1 vs. New 2 in individual SOM-ints. This correlation was strong on Day 1, and strikingly, this correlation was significant across all days of the remapping protocol (Figure 6A, Day 1, p<0.001; Day 2, p<0.001; Day 3, p<0.001; Day 5, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A with statistical tests

claim: When comparing activity suppression in New 1 vs. 'No Task' epochs, there was significant correlation for each cell on Day 1.
source: Even here, when comparing activity suppression in New 1 vs. 'No Task' epochs, we found significant correlation for each cell on Day 1, indicating that the functional inhibitory network structure for these two very different behavioral epochs is very similar.
evidence: Analysis of correlation data

claim: The correlation between New 1 and 'No Task' activity suppression was not significant on Days 2–5.
source: We also measured correlation in activity suppression throughout the 5-day protocol. Although the correlation was significant on Day 1 (Figure 6B, p<0.001), it was not on Days 2–5.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B with statistical tests

claim: Each SOM-int exhibits a consistent degree of activity suppression across multiple new environments.
source: These results show that each cell exhibits a consistent degree of activity suppression across multiple new environments.
evidence: Summary of correlation findings

claim: Cells stratified by the magnitude of their initial suppression continue to be stratified by activity suppression across the 5-day remapping protocol.
source: Cells stratified by the magnitude of their initial suppression continue to be stratified by activity suppression across the 5-day remapping protocol, with the most strongly suppressed on Day 1 remaining the most suppressed on Day 5, while the least suppressed remain the least suppressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: There was no difference in activity suppression between cells with somata in SO vs. SP.
source: We found no difference in activity suppression between cells with somata in SO vs. SP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, p=0.38), suggesting that each cell's magnitude of activity suppression was not defined by cell-type, at least at the level of classification of OLM and bistratified interneurons.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C with statistical test

claim: Baseline fluorescence exhibited no relationship to activity suppression.
source: We also found that baseline fluorescence (which could be indicative of basal firing rate, with strong caveats) exhibited no relationship to activity suppression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D

claim: There was no relationship between soma area and activity suppression.
source: There was no relationship between soma area and activity suppression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, p>0.99).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E with statistical test

claim: There was no difference in activity suppression between locomotion-correlated and anti-correlated SOM-int populations.
source: However, there was no difference in activity suppression between the two (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, p>0.99).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F with statistical test

claim: There was no relationship between cell-cell distance and activity suppression.
source: However, there was no relationship between cell-cell distance and activity suppression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I

claim: Closer cells have more similar activity.
source: We did, however, find that closer cells have more similar activity, although the relationship was weak (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J

claim: There is general preservation of activity relationships between cells in Fam and New.
source: In an example animal, in the matrix of cell-cell activity comparisons, there is general preservation of activity relationships between cells in Fam and New (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: Correlation in cell-cell activity was found when looking at Fam vs. New, New 1 vs. New 2, Fam vs. No Task, and New vs. No Task.
source: Indeed, we found correlation in cell-cell activity when looking at Fam vs. New, New 1 vs. New 2, Fam vs. No Task, and New vs. No Task (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–G

claim: Cell pairs with dissimilar amounts of activity suppression in New also had lower activity correlations in Fam.
source: We found that cell pairs with dissimilar amounts of activity suppression in New also had lower activity correlations in Fam (Figure 6—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2H

claim: Cell pairs with more similar activity had significantly less activity suppression.
source: We found that cell pairs with more similar activity had significantly less activity suppression, although this relationship was relatively weak (Figure 6—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2I

claim: Activity structure based on cell-pair activity correlation was stable across 5 days of exposure in Fam, New, and 'No Task'.
source: Finally, we found that activity structure based on cell-pair activity correlation was stable across 5 days of exposure in Fam, New, and 'No Task' (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3

claim: The activity of SOM- and PV-ints was initially strongly suppressed upon exposure to a novel virtual environment.
source: We found that the activity of SOM- and PV-ints was initially strongly suppressed upon exposure to a novel virtual environment, and that activity recovered as animals learned to adapt a goal-directed spatial navigation task to this new environment.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: SOM-int and PV-int activity recovered as animals learned to adapt a goal-directed spatial navigation task to the new environment.
source: We found that the activity of SOM- and PV-ints was initially strongly suppressed upon exposure to a novel virtual environment, and that activity recovered as animals learned to adapt a goal-directed spatial navigation task to this new environment.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: There was a persistent functional network structure in the transition from familiar to novel environments for SOM-ints.
source: Furthermore for SOM-ints, there was a persistent functional network structure in the transition from familiar to novel environments.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: Each SOM-int exhibited a characteristic amount of activity suppression in multiple new environments, as well as in a drastically different 'No Task' environment.
source: Each SOM-int exhibited a characteristic amount of activity suppression in multiple new environments, as well as in a drastically different 'No Task' environment where there was no recovery of task performance.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: Entering new environments triggers decreased network inhibition, which then gradually recovers over the course of learning to stabilize the network.
source: Our findings are consistent with a model in which entering new environments triggers decreased network inhibition, which then gradually recovers over the course of learning to stabilize the network (Frank et al., 2004; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: Interpretation of findings with citation support

claim: Suppression of both dendrite- and soma-targeting interneurons suggests general disinhibition of postsynaptic pyramidal neurons during spatial exploration in this task.
source: We found suppression of both dendrite- and soma-targeting interneurons (SOM- and PV-ints, respectively), suggesting general disinhibition of postsynaptic pyramidal neurons during spatial exploration in this task, rather than subregion-specific changes (Chen et al., 2015; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Sheffield et al., 2017).
evidence: Interpretation of findings with citation support

claim: Loss in inhibition may act as a permissive gate for learning by enhancing synaptic plasticity in the pyramidal neurons.
source: This loss in inhibition may act as a permissive gate for learning by enhancing synaptic plasticity in the pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Speculation based on findings

claim: The actual inhibitory drive onto pyramidal neurons during spatial exploration remains unknown.
source: However, an important limitation of our data is that, while we measured calcium activity in interneuronal somata and neurites (axonal and dendritic), the actual inhibitory drive onto pyramidal neurons during spatial exploration remains unknown.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation

claim: In the 'No Task' epoch, the normal positive correlation between locomotion and interneuronal activity was greatly weakened.
source: It was striking that, in the 'No Task' epoch, the normal positive correlation between locomotion and interneuronal activity was greatly weakened: even though mice ran on the ball at high speed, SOM- and PV-int activity remained low.
evidence: Observation from experimental data

claim: The low interneuron activity state may signify a network that is primed for learning, rather than an indication of novelty.
source: Thus, the low interneuron activity state may signify a network that is primed for learning, rather than an indication of novelty.
evidence: Speculation based on findings

claim: Switching animals to new environments triggers a few minutes of activity suppression and the formation of new place cell maps on the same timescale.
source: In both real world and VR experiments, switching animals to new environments triggers a few minutes of activity suppression and the formation of new place cell maps on the same timescale (Frank et al., 2004; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Muller and Kubie, 1987; Nitz and McNaughton, 2004; Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: In a learning task with no global remapping where freely moving rats learned new goal locations in a familiar environment, fast-spiking putative interneurons both increased and decreased activity as performance increased.
source: By contrast, in a learning task with no global remapping where freely moving rats learned new goal locations in a familiar environment, fast-spiking putative interneurons both increased and decreased activity as performance increased (Dupret et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dupret et al., 2013

claim: Network activity structure (measured as pairwise cell-cell activity) is stable across different contexts, including the drastically different 'No Task' epoch.
source: First, network activity structure (measured as pairwise cell-cell activity) is stable across different contexts, including the drastically different 'No Task' epoch.
evidence: Summary of findings

claim: Interneuron activity dynamics were stable on a cell-by-cell basis, with each interneuron having a consistent level of activity suppression, both across multiple new environments and in the 'No Task' epoch.
source: Second, interneuron activity dynamics were stable on a cell-by-cell basis, with each interneuron having a consistent level of activity suppression, both across multiple new environments and in the 'No Task' epoch.
evidence: Summary of findings

claim: The underlying inhibitory circuit infrastructure may serve to shape information encoding in the local pyramidal cell network.
source: These findings reveal an underlying inhibitory circuit infrastructure that may serve to shape information encoding in the local pyramidal cell network.
evidence: Interpretation of findings

claim: Pyramidal neurons downstream of strongly suppressed interneurons are more likely to express plasticity.
source: Pyramidal neurons downstream of strongly suppressed interneurons are more likely to express plasticity, as a direct result of increased activity due to release of inhibition.
evidence: Speculation based on findings

claim: Functionally diverse, but consistent, inhibitory structure may act as a mechanism to balance stability with plasticity.
source: Thus, this functionally diverse, but consistent, inhibitory structure may act as a mechanism to address a fundamental tradeoff in neuronal network function: balancing stability with plasticity (Abraham and Robins, 2005; McClelland et al., 1995; McCloskey and Cohen, 1989).
evidence: Speculation based on findings with citation support

claim: In the hippocampus, PV-expressing basket cells preferentially inhibit deep pyramidal neurons projecting to the amygdala.
source: In the hippocampus, PV-expressing basket cells preferentially inhibit deep pyramidal neurons projecting to the amygdala, while also being more likely to receive excitation from superficial pyramidal neurons or from deep pyramidal neurons projecting to the prefrontal cortex (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: In the medial entorhinal cortex, cholecystokinin-expressing basket cells selectively target pyramidal neurons that project extra-hippocampally.
source: In the medial entorhinal cortex, cholecystokinin-expressing basket cells selectively target pyramidal neurons that project extra-hippocampally (Varga et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Varga et al., 2010

claim: In the hippocampus, interneurons participate in cell assemblies with pyramidal neurons and can share coding properties such as place fields.
